messages.subject: Multi-Method Occupancy//Sampling In Different Locations
parts:
Hi All,

I am a graduate student looking for some help. I am studying the Sierra Nevada red fox in the Oregon Cascades. The species is elusive and has a low abundance, making them hard to detect. I set camera traps using a random stratified sampling design, and did scat surveys, when going to and from the camera stations (~2 surveys/sampling period at different times but across the same space). Because I did not always have cameras where I was surveying for scats, how do you think I can integrate these 2 methods into one model to compare detection probabilities (effectiveness) of each method?

Eventually, I hope to combine my detections from these two methods to inform my single species occupancy models. 

I have looked into Nichols (2008) but am unsure if this model would work considering the methods I used were not done in the same location. Is there any way, I can integrate these two methods into one model and compare their detection probabilities? Any examples you can point me towards? 

Thanks for your help! 

Marwa

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: AW: [unmarked] Multi-Method Occupancy//Sampling In Different Locations
parts:
Dear Marwa,

 

the main thing to consider is how to avoid spatial mis-aligment of these two sources of information about fox occurrence. Occupancy probability is scale-dependent and the spatial scales of your two types of surveys are different. The spatial scale associated with the camera trap data is either the (small) area that is ‘seen’ by a trap (e.g., a handful of m2) or the (large) area of a homerange of your target species, within which the camera trap is set up. Or something in between ? (Isn’t there some paper about this somewhere ?)

 

In contrast, the spatial scale associated with your scat surveys is the strip of area that you look at while moving from one trap to the next (or the size of the homerange of the species that can leave scat along your transect ?).

 

I think that as a first attempt, I’d break apart your scat surveys into a series of smaller ‘sites’, with size approximately equal to the size of the area seen by a camtrap. That way, you should achieve a reconciliation of the spatial scale of the two surveys. Then, I’d of course fit a different intercept for the detection model for the two types of surveys, but a shared occupancy model, since your surveys are in the same area. You could fit this model simply using occu() in unmarked.

 

One thing that you’d ignore though is possible spatial autocorrelation in the detections along your scat transect --- for this, the “tiger on trails” models by Hines (see this) could be used. But: this model is only available in software PRESENCE and probably MARK, but not in unmarked. In Bayesian software such as JAGS or NIMBLE, you could specify an integrated model with a tiger on trails component for the suitably formatted scat data and a standard occupancy component for the camtrap data.

 

Best regards  -- Marc

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Multi-Method Occupancy//Sampling In Different Locations
parts:
Dear Marwa,
 What Marc said is worth thinking about. But assuming the search route into the camera isn't large relative to a typical animal's home range, I think it would be ok to treat the camera and the scat search as distinct sample events, paired, for the same site. So if you did 2 survey occasions with the camera traps and that produced also 2 scat searches then I think viewing this as 4 sample occasions could be ok -- but with different detection probabilities due to the different method being employed for detection. This "method" variable would just be an observation covariate.  
 regards
any

messages.subject: Re: Multi-Method Occupancy//Sampling In Different Locations
parts:
Hi Jeffrey and Marc,

Sorry it has been a while! Thank you all for your input. It was helpful for leading me in the right direction. I ended up doing a model for scats+cameras with only the method as a covariate, holding occupancy constant. There I can directly look at probability of detection based on survey method. I also have separate models for scat detection and camera detection that include covariates associated with each survey methods.

Thank you again! 

Marwa
